```{r}
#| include: false
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 16))

data_dir <- "../../Data sets from Modelling Survival Data in Medical Research, 4th edition"

# Same set-up as Lecture 12 (identical object names, labels and reference levels)
# Liver transplant recipients (Collett Example 12.1)
liver <- read.table(file.path(data_dir, "Survival of liver transplant recipients.dat"), header = TRUE)
liver <- liver |>
  mutate(gender = factor(gender, 1:2, c("Male", "Female")),
         disease = factor(disease, 1:3, c("PBC", "PSC", "ALD")),
         disease = relevel(disease, ref = "ALD"),
         cause = factor(cof, 0:4, c("censored", "rejection", "thrombosis", "recurrent disease", "other")),
         time_y = time / 365.25)

# MGUS: patients with missing hgb are dropped (as in Lecture 12)
mgus <- mgus2 |>
  filter(!is.na(hgb)) |>
  mutate(etime = ifelse(pstat == 1, ptime, futime),
         event = factor(case_when(pstat == 1 ~ 1, death == 1 ~ 2, TRUE ~ 0),
                        levels = 0:2, labels = c("censored", "progression", "death")))
for (v in names(mgus)) attr(mgus[[v]], "label") <- NULL
```

## Recap (Lecture 12)

Each subject experiences **one** of $m$ event types $k = 1, \dots, m$ (or is censored). Details and the $1-\text{KM}$ bias are in Lecture 12; what we need here:

- **Cause-specific hazard** $h_k(t)$, cumulative $H_k(t)$, overall survival $S(t) = \exp\{-\sum_k H_k(t)\}$
- **Cumulative incidence** $\mathrm{CIF}_k(t) = P(T \le t, C = k) = \int_0^t S(u-)\, h_k(u)\, du$ depends on **all** $h_k$, not only on $h_k$
- Today's question: how do covariates affect the *hazard* of cause $k$, and how do they affect the *probability* $\mathrm{CIF}_k(t)$?

# Two running examples

## Example 1: liver transplant recipients

Collett Example 12.1: $n =$ `r nrow(liver)` adults, first elective liver transplant, time to **graft failure**; causes: rejection, thrombosis, recurrent disease, other. Deaths with a functioning graft are censored in this data set.

```{r}
liver |> select(patient, age, gender, disease, time, status, cof) |> head(4)
liver |> count(cause) |> mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
```

Covariates: `age` (years), `gender`, `disease` (PBC, PSC, ALD; reference ALD). Time is in days.

::: {.callout-note}
We define events from `cof` (0 = censored, 1 to 4 = causes). In the file, `status` and `cof` disagree for `r sum((liver$status > 0) != (liver$cof > 0))` of `r nrow(liver)` patients (`r sum(liver$status > 0 & liver$cof == 0)` with `status` = 1 but `cof` = 0, `r sum(liver$status == 0 & liver$cof > 0)` the reverse); we use `cof`.
:::

## Example 2: MGUS, progression or death

`mgus2` (Mayo Clinic): `r nrow(mgus2)` patients with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, a premalignant plasma-cell condition. Event of interest: **progression** to a plasma cell malignancy. **Competing event**: death without progression (common in this elderly cohort).

```{r}
mgus |> count(event) |> mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
```

Time `etime` in months from diagnosis; covariates `age`, `sex`, `hgb` (haemoglobin, g/dl). `r nrow(mgus2) - nrow(mgus)` patients with missing `hgb` are dropped (same data as in Lecture 12), leaving `r nrow(mgus)`.

::: {.callout-tip}
We check the coding by inspection: `pstat = 1` is progression (time `ptime`); otherwise follow-up ends at `futime` with `death` 1/0.
:::

## CIFs for MGUS by sex

Needed to interpret the sex effects below (the in-class exercise of Lecture 12 asks for the same plot).

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.3
tidycmprsk::cuminc(Surv(etime, event) ~ sex, data = mgus) |>
  ggcuminc(outcome = c("progression", "death")) +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  labs(x = "Months since diagnosis", y = "Cumulative incidence") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
ci_sex <- tidycmprsk::tidy(tidycmprsk::cuminc(Surv(etime, event) ~ sex, data = mgus), times = 120)
cs <- \(o, g) ci_sex |> filter(outcome == o, strata == g) |> pull(estimate)
```

At 10 years the CIF of death is `r round(cs("death", "M"), 2)` in men and `r round(cs("death", "F"), 2)` in women; for progression it is `r round(cs("progression", "M"), 2)` and `r round(cs("progression", "F"), 2)`.

# Cause-specific Cox models

## Idea: one Cox model per cause

For cause $k$ the hazard for subject $i$ is (Collett Section 12.4)

$$h_{ik}(t) = \exp(\boldsymbol\beta_k^{cs\prime} \mathbf{x}_i)\, h_{0k}(t)$$

**Recipe**: for each cause $k$ in turn

1. event = cause $k$
2. everyone who has a **competing** event is **censored** at that time
3. fit `coxph()` as usual

. . .

- Separate $\boldsymbol\beta_k^{cs}$ and baseline $h_{0k}$ for each cause
- Standard software, standard PH checks, time-dependent covariates all work
- Hazard ratio: effect on the **rate of cause $k$ among those still event-free** (alive, no event of any type so far)

## Cause-specific Cox in R: MGUS

```{r}
cs_prog <- coxph(Surv(etime, event == "progression") ~ age + sex + hgb, data = mgus)
cs_death <- coxph(Surv(etime, event == "death") ~ age + sex + hgb, data = mgus)
```

```{r}
#| output-location: column
library(gtsummary)
tbl_merge(
  list(tbl_regression(cs_prog, exponentiate = TRUE),
       tbl_regression(cs_death, exponentiate = TRUE)),
  tab_spanner = c("**Progression**", "**Death**")
)
```

## Interpreting the MGUS cause-specific models

```{r}
#| include: false
cp <- exp(coef(cs_prog)); cd <- exp(coef(cs_death))
pp <- summary(cs_prog)$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
pd <- summary(cs_death)$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
fp <- \(x) ifelse(x < 0.001, "< 0.001", paste("=", round(x, 3)))
```

- **Progression**: each g/dl higher haemoglobin changes the progression hazard by a factor `r round(cp["hgb"], 2)` (p = `r round(pp["hgb"], 3)`), among patients alive and progression-free. Age: HR `r round(cp["age"], 2)` per year (p = `r round(pp["age"], 3)`); men vs women: HR `r round(cp["sexM"], 2)` (p = `r round(pp["sexM"], 3)`).
- **Death**: HR `r round(cd["age"], 2)` per year of age (`r round(cd["age"]^10, 1)` per 10 years, p `r fp(pd["age"])`), men `r round(cd["sexM"], 2)` times the death rate of women (p `r fp(pd["sexM"])`), haemoglobin HR `r round(cd["hgb"], 2)` per g/dl (p `r fp(pd["hgb"])`).

. . .

Read together: compare the age HR for death with that for progression above (sizes and p-values); both models are needed to understand the disease course.

## Liver data: four cause-specific models

```{r}
causes <- c("rejection", "thrombosis", "recurrent disease", "other")
cs_liver <- map(causes, \(k) coxph(Surv(time, cause == k) ~ age + gender + disease, data = liver)) |>
  set_names(causes)
map_dfr(cs_liver, broom::tidy, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE, .id = "cause") |>
  filter(term != "age") |>
  transmute(cause, term, HR = round(estimate, 2),
            CI = str_c(round(conf.low, 2), " to ", round(conf.high, 2)), p = round(p.value, 3))
```

(Age: see next slide.) Compare Collett Table 12.5 (the liver data and the hazard ratios there are the same).

## Liver: what do these say?

```{r}
#| include: false
tl <- map_dfr(cs_liver, broom::tidy, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE, .id = "cause")
g <- \(k, t) tl |> filter(cause == k, term == t)
```

- **Thrombosis**: PBC has hazard `r round(g("thrombosis", "diseasePBC")$estimate, 2)` times that of ALD (95% CI `r round(g("thrombosis", "diseasePBC")$conf.low, 2)` to `r round(g("thrombosis", "diseasePBC")$conf.high, 2)`).
- **Recurrent disease**: PBC HR `r round(g("recurrent disease", "diseasePBC")$estimate, 2)` (CI `r round(g("recurrent disease", "diseasePBC")$conf.low, 2)` to `r round(g("recurrent disease", "diseasePBC")$conf.high, 2)`), i.e. a `r ifelse(g("recurrent disease", "diseasePBC")$estimate < 1, "lower", "higher")` rate than ALD; PSC HR `r round(g("recurrent disease", "diseasePSC")$estimate, 2)`.
- **Other causes**: age HR `r round(g("other", "age")$estimate, 2)` per year (CI `r round(g("other", "age")$conf.low, 2)` to `r round(g("other", "age")$conf.high, 2)`); the rate of failure from other causes `r ifelse(g("other", "age")$estimate > 1, "increases", "decreases")` with age.
- **Rejection**: only `r sum(liver$cause == "rejection")` events, so wide intervals.

Different causes have different risk factors: this is the **etiological** insight.

## Cause-specific models: what they do and do not say

::: {.callout-note}
**Good for**: aetiology ("does X change the biological rate of cause $k$?"), comparing effects across causes, and mechanisms.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Limitations**

- Censoring at the competing event relies on **independence** between causes; this cannot be tested from the data (Collett, Section 12.4)
- $\hat\beta_k^{cs}$ does not tell the effect on the **probability** of cause $k$: $\mathrm{CIF}_k(t)$ depends on all $h_{k'}$
- A covariate that raises the competing hazard lowers the CIF for cause $k$ while leaving $h_k$ unchanged
:::

# Subdistribution hazard and Fine–Gray

## The idea: model the CIF directly

Is there a hazard whose Cox-type model maps straight to $\mathrm{CIF}_k(t)$? Define the **subdistribution hazard**

$$h^{sub}_k(t) = -\frac{d}{dt}\log\{1 - \mathrm{CIF}_k(t)\}= \lim_{\delta t \to 0}\frac{P(t \le T < t+\delta t, C = k \mid T \ge t \text{ or } \{T < t \text{ and } C \ne k\})}{\delta t}$$

. . .

Fine and Gray (1999) assume

$$h^{sub}_{ik}(t) = \exp(\boldsymbol\beta_k^{sub\prime} \mathbf{x}_i)\, h^{sub}_{0k}(t) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathrm{CIF}_{ik}(t) = 1 - \{1 - \mathrm{CIF}_{0k}(t)\}^{\exp(\boldsymbol\beta_k^{sub\prime} \mathbf{x}_i)}$$

A one-to-one link between the covariates and the CIF, like $S(t) = \exp\{-H(t)\}$ in the one-event case.

## The risk set is different

At an event time of cause $k$:

| | Cause-specific Cox | Fine–Gray |
|---|---|---|
| Still event-free | in risk set | in risk set |
| Had a **competing** event earlier | removed (censored) | **kept**, with weight $w < 1$ |
| Censored earlier | removed | removed |

. . .

Weights (Collett Section 12.5.1): $w_{hl}(t) = \hat S_c(t) / \hat S_c(\min\{t, t_l\})$, where $\hat S_c$ is the Kaplan–Meier estimate of the **censoring** distribution. People who had a competing event keep contributing with declining weight.

::: {.callout-warning}
The "at risk" set contains people who cannot get cause $k$ any more. The subhazard is therefore **not** a rate in the usual sense, and the $\beta_k^{sub}$ are best read via their effect on $\mathrm{CIF}_k(t)$.
:::

## Fine–Gray in R: `tidycmprsk::crr()`

```{r}
fg_prog <- tidycmprsk::crr(Surv(etime, event) ~ age + sex + hgb, data = mgus, failcode = "progression")
fg_death <- tidycmprsk::crr(Surv(etime, event) ~ age + sex + hgb, data = mgus, failcode = "death")
fg_prog
```

`event` must be a **factor** with the censoring level first; `failcode` picks the cause. Output is a subdistribution HR (SHR) $\exp(\hat\beta_k^{sub})$.

## The same with `cmprsk::crr()`

The older interface takes times, a cause code, and a covariate **matrix**:

```{r}
X <- model.matrix(~ age + sex + hgb, data = mgus)[, -1]
# explicit event labels instead of numeric factor codes
fstat <- as.character(mgus$event)
fg_prog2 <- cmprsk::crr(ftime = mgus$etime, fstatus = fstat,
                        cov1 = X, failcode = "progression", cencode = "censored")
round(summary(fg_prog2)$conf.int, 3)
```

Same estimates as `tidycmprsk` (which wraps `cmprsk`). `cmprsk::crr` provides `predict()` for CIFs, which we use later.

## MGUS: interpreting Fine–Gray

```{r}
#| include: false
sp <- exp(coef(fg_prog)); sd_ <- exp(coef(fg_death))
psp <- setNames(fg_prog$tidy$p.value, fg_prog$tidy$term)
```

```{r}
#| output-location: column
tbl_merge(
  list(tbl_regression(fg_prog, exponentiate = TRUE),
       tbl_regression(fg_death, exponentiate = TRUE)),
  tab_spanner = c("**Progression**", "**Death**")
)
```

- Progression: SHR for age `r round(sp["age"], 2)` per year (p = `r round(psp["age"], 3)`), compared with the cause-specific HR `r round(cp["age"], 2)`. An SHR below 1 for age means a lower CIF of progression in older patients, which can reflect the higher death rate of the old rather than a protective effect on the progression process.
- Death: SHR for age `r round(sd_["age"], 2)`, men `r round(sd_["sexM"], 2)`; cause-specific HRs were `r round(cd["age"], 2)` and `r round(cd["sexM"], 2)`.

## Cause-specific HR vs subdistribution HR, MGUS

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
bind_rows(
  broom::tidy(cs_prog, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(model = "Cause-specific Cox", cause = "Progression"),
  broom::tidy(fg_prog, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(model = "Fine-Gray", cause = "Progression"),
  broom::tidy(cs_death, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(model = "Cause-specific Cox", cause = "Death"),
  broom::tidy(fg_death, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |> mutate(model = "Fine-Gray", cause = "Death")
) |>
  mutate(term = recode(term, sexM = "sex (M vs F)")) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, term, colour = model, xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = 2) +
  geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~cause, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Hazard ratio (log scale)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
cmp <- \(v) c(cs = cp[v], sub = sp[v])
```

Compare the two sets of intervals per covariate: for death, the cause-specific HR and SHR for age are `r round(cd["age"], 2)` and `r round(sd_["age"], 2)`; for progression, haemoglobin has HR `r round(cp["hgb"], 2)` and SHR `r round(sp["hgb"], 2)`, age has HR `r round(cp["age"], 2)` and SHR `r round(sp["age"], 2)`. Intervals that exclude 1 in one model but not the other show where the two questions give different answers.

# Two models, two questions

## Why can they differ?

$$\mathrm{CIF}_1(t) = \int_0^t \exp\Big\{-\sum_k H_k(u)\Big\}\, h_1(u)\, du$$

- Cause-specific Cox models $h_1$ only
- Fine–Gray models $\mathrm{CIF}_1$, which also involves $h_2$

If a covariate raises $h_2$ (the competing hazard), then:

- the $h_1$ ratio can be $1$ (no direct effect on cause 1)
- but fewer people survive long enough to experience cause 1, so $\mathrm{CIF}_1$ is **lower**: SHR < 1

. . .

The two HRs can differ in size, significance, **and sign**. This is not an error; they answer different questions.

## Where they agree and where they disagree

| Situation | CS HR vs SHR |
|---|---|
| Competing event rare or unrelated to $x$ | similar (e.g. liver data, Collett Table 12.5 vs 12.6) |
| $x$ strongly affects the competing hazard | can differ a lot, even in direction |
| Heavy censoring, few competing events | similar |
| MGUS age effect on progression | CS HR `r round(cp["age"], 2)` vs SHR `r round(sp["age"], 2)` |

Liver data, thrombosis, PBC vs ALD:

```{r}
fg_liver <- map(causes, \(k) tidycmprsk::crr(Surv(time, cause) ~ age + gender + disease, data = liver, failcode = k)) |>
  set_names(causes)
c(cause_specific = exp(coef(cs_liver$thrombosis))[["diseasePBC"]],
  fine_gray = exp(coef(fg_liver$thrombosis))[["diseasePBC"]]) |> round(2)
```

## Which model? A guide

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Cause-specific hazard**

- Question: *"What is the effect of $x$ on the disease process / mechanism?"*
- Aetiology, risk factors, treatment efficacy on the biology
- Hazards are comparable across studies with different competing risks
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Fine–Gray**

- Question: *"What is the effect of $x$ on the absolute risk of cause $k$?"*
- Prediction, risk scores, counselling, health-economic planning
- Directly linked to the CIF
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
**Recommendation**: report **both**, plus CIF plots for the main groups (Austin, Lee and Fine 2016). The cause-specific results tell you why; the CIF tells you how much. Decide the primary analysis **before** seeing the data.
:::

## Pitfalls (regression)

- Fine–Gray SHR is **not** a cause-specific HR. Do not say "rate among those at risk".
- Do not interpret a non-significant SHR as "no effect on the biology of cause $k$".
- Each cause needs its own model: an effect on cause 1 says nothing about cause 2.
- Fine–Gray additionally uses the censoring distribution in its weights.

# Predicting cumulative incidence

## From Fine–Gray: `predict()` for a profile

Patient profile: a 70-year-old man with hgb 13 g/dl, versus a woman of the same age and hgb.

```{r}
X <- model.matrix(~ age + sex + hgb, data = mgus)[, -1]
fg_cm <- cmprsk::crr(mgus$etime, fstat, cov1 = X, failcode = "progression", cencode = "censored")
newx <- rbind(Male = c(age = 70, sexM = 1, hgb = 13),
              Female = c(age = 70, sexM = 0, hgb = 13))
pr <- predict(fg_cm, cov1 = newx)   # first column: time; then one CIF per row
head(pr, 3)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
at <- \(m, tt) approx(pr[, 1], pr[, m + 1], xout = tt, method = "constant", f = 0, rule = 2)$y
```

At 10 years (120 months): man `r round(at(1, 120), 3)`, woman `r round(at(2, 120), 3)` (progression).

## From cause-specific models: combine them

No single `predict()` gives a CIF from cause-specific models; assemble it from the pieces

$$\widehat{\mathrm{CIF}}_k(t \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sum_{t_l \le t} \hat S(t_l- \mid \mathbf{x})\, \Delta \hat H_k(t_l \mid \mathbf{x})$$

1. `survfit(coxph_k, newdata)` gives $\hat H_k(t \mid \mathbf{x})$ for each cause
2. $\hat S(t) = \exp\{-\hat H_1(t) - \hat H_2(t)\}$ (all-cause survival)
3. Accumulate $\hat S(t_l-)\,\Delta \hat H_k(t_l)$

(`riskRegression::CSC()` with `predict()` automates this.)

## Worked code: CIFs from cause-specific models

```{r}
cif_cs <- function(fits, newdata, times) {
  # cumulative hazard of each cause on a common time grid
  H <- sapply(fits, \(f) {
    sf <- survfit(f, newdata = newdata)
    stepfun(sf$time, c(0, sf$cumhaz))(times)
  })
  S_all <- exp(-rowSums(H))
  S_prev <- c(1, head(S_all, -1))
  apply(H, 2, \(h) cumsum(S_prev * diff(c(0, h))))
}
grid <- seq(0, 300, by = 1)
nd <- data.frame(age = 70, sex = "M", hgb = 13)
F_cs <- cif_cs(list(progression = cs_prog, death = cs_death), nd, grid)
round(F_cs[grid == 120, ], 3)
```

At 120 months for the 70-year-old man with hgb 13: progression `r round(F_cs[grid == 120, "progression"], 3)`, death `r round(F_cs[grid == 120, "death"], 3)`.

## Comparing the two predictions

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.3
tibble(time = grid, `Cause-specific Cox (combined)` = F_cs[, "progression"],
       `Fine-Gray` = at(1, grid)) |>
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "method", values_to = "cif") |>
  ggplot(aes(time, cif, colour = method)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Months since diagnosis", y = "Cumulative incidence of progression",
       colour = NULL, title = "70-year-old man, hgb 13 g/dl") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Both are estimates of the same $\mathrm{CIF}_1(t \mid \mathbf{x})$; they use different model assumptions (PH for the cause-specific hazards vs PH for the subhazard) and so can differ somewhat.

## Patient profiles: both causes, men vs women

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.3
nd2 <- data.frame(age = 70, sex = c("M", "F"), hgb = 13)
out <- map_dfr(1:2, \(i) {
  F <- cif_cs(list(progression = cs_prog, death = cs_death), nd2[i, ], grid)
  as_tibble(F) |> mutate(time = grid, sex = nd2$sex[i])
}) |> pivot_longer(c(progression, death), names_to = "cause", values_to = "cif")
ggplot(out, aes(time, cif, colour = sex, linetype = cause)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Months since diagnosis", y = "Cumulative incidence", colour = "Sex",
       title = "Cause-specific Cox models, age 70, hgb 13") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Death dominates for men. The CIFs of the two causes plus $\hat S(t)$ always sum to 1.

## Prediction with `tidycmprsk`

```{r}
nd_m <- data.frame(age = 70, sex = factor("M", levels = c("F", "M")), hgb = 13,
                   etime = 1, event = factor("censored", levels(mgus$event)))
predict(fg_prog, times = c(60, 120, 240), newdata = nd_m) |> unlist() |> round(3)
```

`newdata` must also contain the outcome columns (dummy values are fine). The same quantity as `predict.crr` above (progression CIF at 5, 10, 20 years). Report **absolute risks** with a confidence interval where possible; the CIF is easier to communicate to a patient than any HR.

## Liver data: a prediction example

Fine–Gray model for **recurrent disease**: 55-year-old woman, by primary disease (CIF at 1, 3 and 6 years).

```{r}
nd <- expand_grid(age = 55, gender = "Female", disease = c("ALD", "PBC", "PSC")) |>
  mutate(gender = factor(gender, levels(liver$gender)), disease = factor(disease, levels(liver$disease)),
         time = 1, cause = factor("censored", levels(liver$cause)))
pr_l <- predict(fg_liver[["recurrent disease"]], times = c(365, 1095, 2190), newdata = nd)
tibble(disease = nd$disease, year1 = pr_l[[1]], year3 = pr_l[[2]], year6 = pr_l[[3]]) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("year"), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

# Checking and extensions

## Checking proportional hazards

**Cause-specific Cox**: as in Lecture 6, `cox.zph()` per cause.

```{r}
#| output-location: column
cox.zph(cs_death)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
zp <- cox.zph(cs_death)$table[, "p"]
fp <- \(x) ifelse(x < 0.001, "< 0.001", paste("=", round(x, 3)))
```

For death in MGUS the p-values of the PH tests are: `r str_c(names(zp), " ", fp(zp), collapse = ", ")`. Values below 0.05 indicate that the effect of that covariate changes over time.

. . .

**Fine–Gray**: the PH assumption is on the subhazard. A simple check: add a covariate-by-time interaction in `cmprsk::crr`:

```{r}
fg_tv <- cmprsk::crr(mgus$etime, fstat, cov1 = X[, "hgb", drop = FALSE],
                     cov2 = X[, "age", drop = FALSE], tf = function(t) log(t),
                     failcode = "death", cencode = "censored")
round(summary(fg_tv)$coef, 3)
```

The row `age*tf1` (log-time interaction) tests whether the age effect on the death CIF changes over time; a coefficient clearly different from zero suggests non-PH. Residual plots and extensions such as time-dependent effects (Collett Section 12.6) apply per cause.

## Beyond Fine–Gray: direct binomial and pseudo-values

Another way to regress on the CIF at fixed times $t_0$: model $P(T \le t_0, C = k \mid \mathbf{x})$ directly with a link function (**direct binomial regression**) or via **pseudo-values** computed from the Aalen–Johansen estimator and then GLM or GEE. Useful when PH for the subhazard fails; not covered further here.

## What competing risks mean for treatment effects

Constant-hazard CIF formula: see Lecture 12. Suppose treatment **lowers** the hazard of cause 1 but **raises** the hazard of cause 2 (e.g. a drug against cancer progression with a cardiac side-effect).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.8
cif1 <- \(h1, h2, t) h1 / (h1 + h2) * (1 - exp(-(h1 + h2) * t))   # constant hazards, see Lecture 12
t <- seq(0, 20, 0.1)
expand_grid(t = t, arm = c("Control", "Treatment")) |>
  mutate(h1 = ifelse(arm == "Control", 0.10, 0.05), h2 = ifelse(arm == "Control", 0.02, 0.06),
         `Cause 1` = cif1(h1, h2, t), `Cause 2` = cif1(h2, h1, t)) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("Cause"), names_to = "cause", values_to = "CIF") |>
  ggplot(aes(t, CIF, colour = arm)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~cause) + labs(x = "Time", y = "Cumulative incidence", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

*Illustrative constant hazards (cause 1: 0.10 vs 0.05; cause 2: 0.02 vs 0.06 per unit time).*

- Cause-specific HRs: 0.5 for cause 1, 3 for cause 2. A trade-off to **report separately**.
- Do not summarise with one "composite" HR without looking at its components.
- Whether the treatment is "good" depends on how serious each cause is: weigh the CIFs, or use all-cause survival.

## Sample size: events per cause

- Power is driven by **number of events of each cause**, not by $n$
- Rule of thumb for Cox models: about 10 events per parameter, *per cause model*
- Liver data: $n =$ `r nrow(liver)`, but

```{r}
liver |> filter(cause != "censored") |> count(cause)
```

- The 3-level `disease` plus `age` and `gender` is 4 parameters; with few rejections the models are barely estimable
- Rare causes: reduce the model or group causes, only if clinically sensible
- Heavy censoring and competing events both reduce the information on cause $k$

# Wrap-up

## Take-home messages

- **Cause-specific Cox**: one model per cause, others censored; HR = effect on the rate among those still event-free; answers aetiological questions
- **Fine–Gray**: subdistribution hazard, competing-event subjects stay in the (weighted) risk set; SHR = effect on the **CIF**; answers prediction and absolute-risk questions
- The two can differ in size and **direction**; neither is wrong
- **Report both**, together with CIF plots; predict CIFs for patient profiles
- Check PH in each model; watch the number of **events per cause**
- Alternative: direct binomial / pseudo-value regression for the CIF

**Next lecture**: recurrent events and event history analysis (Collett, Chapter 13).

**Reading**: Collett, Chapter 12, Sections 12.4 to 12.6 (modelling cause-specific hazards, the Fine and Gray model, model checking). Further: Austin, Lee and Fine (2016), *Circulation* 133:601–609; Fine and Gray (1999), *JASA* 94:496–509.
